project_description:
Mollet is a local robotics workbench that turns a behavior a developer wants to see into an auditable temporal condition. Reward curves can indicate that something changed, while video alone makes it difficult to repeat the same numeric check and identify exactly when the behavior held. In Mollet, a developer describes the target behavior in natural language. A Meta language model proposes a restricted JSON condition, SAM supplies frame-level robot locations, and a deterministic evaluator checks the condition against the original synchronized telemetry. The result is PASS, FAIL, or UNKNOWN, with the matching time interval and evidence shown beside the video.

In our verified H1 stair example, the proposed condition required up-axis alignment of at least 0.8 to begin within eight seconds and hold for 0.5 seconds. The local evaluator returned PASS for 0.0 to 0.5 seconds. A reviewer then changed the hold to eight seconds, received PASS for 0.0 to 8.0 seconds, exported the condition, loaded it again, and confirmed that its values were preserved while the previous approval was cleared. A manually authored full-duration Go2 condition returned FAIL.

Mollet preserves request and response hashes, video and state provenance, review state, and the evaluation result in the exported JSON. This makes a model suggestion editable and replayable without treating it as ground truth. Mollet builds on our pre-existing RL diagnosis foundation and stair recordings. The hackathon work adds Meta-powered condition authoring, SAM location binding, temporal evaluation, review reset, export round-trip, and saved-response replay.
meta_products:
Mollet uses Muse Spark 1.3 and SAM 3.1 through the Meta Responses API. We completed one authenticated Spark call using a natural-language behavior request plus state JSON. Spark returned a constrained condition for the H1 stair recording: up_axis_z greater than or equal to 0.8, an eight-second start deadline, and a 0.5-second hold. Spark did not analyze the raw video in this verified call. We also completed one SAM 3.1 call on the original H1 video. It returned robot boxes for 624 of 625 samples; this is response coverage, not a measurement of tracking accuracy.

Mollet combines those outputs with the original synchronized telemetry. SAM boxes show where the robot is in each available frame, while the local evaluator decides whether the Spark-authored condition holds and reports PASS, FAIL, or UNKNOWN. Reviewers can edit the condition, rerun it, approve its meaning locally, and export the condition with provenance and hashes. Loading an edited export preserves the values and clears the old approval so that a changed condition must be reviewed again.

For the current three-minute demo, Mollet verifies and replays the saved responses from those two authenticated calls, then shows the current workflow in Chrome. Replay checks the source hashes and labels whether local raw provider files were verified or only the checked-in evidence index was available; it makes no new model call. The related suite passed 142 CPU tests and 10 Chrome checks. We also implemented code paths for video-grounded hypotheses, Spark reflection, and correction proposals; the submitted evidence does not claim a new call, retraining run, or measured recovery improvement from those paths.
why_meta:
Meta's models give Mollet two complementary signals needed for a useful robotics review loop. Muse Spark turns an imprecise request such as maintaining upright alignment on stairs into a small, editable JSON contract with a metric, threshold, deadline, and hold duration. SAM connects that contract to visible robot locations across the source video. The synchronized telemetry then remains the deterministic basis for PASS, FAIL, or UNKNOWN.

This separation matters in robotics because a plausible model response is not enough to establish that a physical behavior occurred. A reviewer needs to see what was proposed, where the robot was, which original measurements were checked, and when the condition held or failed. Mollet keeps each role inspectable: Spark helps author the test, SAM grounds the video view, fixed local rules compute the verdict, and a reviewer controls semantic approval. Missing evidence stays UNKNOWN instead of being converted into a pass.

Our authenticated runs showed that these Meta outputs can be joined to 625 original H1 state samples, replayed with verified receipts and hashes, edited, and exported without changing the underlying telemetry. This makes Meta's models useful as auditable interfaces between human intent, visual context, and repeatable robot evaluation. We do not treat either model as the final authority or claim that the current evidence measures tracking accuracy, generalization, training gains, or recovery improvement.
verified_claims: One authenticated Muse Spark 1.3 call completed from a natural-language request plus state JSON.
One authenticated SAM 3.1 call completed on the original H1 video.
The Spark condition was up_axis_z >= 0.8 with an eight-second start deadline and a 0.5-second hold; deterministic evaluation returned PASS from 0.0 to 0.5 seconds.
The H1 evidence contains 625 original state samples and SAM boxes for 624 samples; the ratio describes response coverage, not tracking accuracy.
A user-edited eight-second hold returned PASS from 0.0 to 8.0 seconds, and export round-trip preserved values while clearing prior approval.
A manually authored full-duration 12.48-second Go2 condition returned FAIL and was not a new model result.
The related local verification passed 142 CPU tests and 10 Chrome checks.
The three-minute demo uses verified saved historical responses from the two authenticated calls and current Chrome footage; replay made no new model call.
limitations: The verified Spark call used natural language plus state JSON; it did not analyze raw video.
The model outputs are suggestions and visual grounding, not the final verdict, human approval, or confirmed reward correction.
Tracking accuracy, cross-task generalization, time savings, and buyer impact were not measured.

Video-grounded hypothesis, reflection, and correction-proposal code paths were implemented, but the submitted evidence contains no new calls, retraining, applied correction, or measured recovery improvement from those paths.

The RL diagnosis foundation and stair recordings predate the hackathon; the new contribution is the Meta condition-authoring, location-binding, temporal evaluation, review, export, and replay workflow.
